catalog_quote: Also relevant are external circumstances, viz. whether the syllable is final or not in the morpheme and, when morphemes are combined into larger units, whether the syllable is stressed or not. [p.69] ... Etic tones a--n occur in fully stressed syllables. Etic tones o---s occur in non-fully stressed syllables in a close-knit phrase with a following fully stressed syllable: they represent a kind of tonal sandhi (see below). [p.70] ... Except in phrase-final position a tone does not usually have its canonical shape, but tends towards sandhi forms, the more the stress reduction the greater the modification. Typical positions for tonal sandhi are the first element in a compound and the first element in a reduplicate. ... The forms just cited display what might be called the first degree of stress reduction, in which vowels retain their distinctive quality but length distinctions tend to be neutralized. ... In the second, or extreme, degree of stress reduction, final consonants are lost and all vowels are replaced by [ə], which can be conveniently interpreted phonemically as (short) /a/, and all tonal distinctions are lost, the etic pitch corresponding more or less to q in the Table of etic tones above. [p.72] ... Non-final syllables in polysyllabic morphemes are subject to stress reduction, with SatM syllables containing /ə/ being treated as showing the second degree of stress reduction and having neutral tone (phonetically about q or s of Table III above) [p.73]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Southern Thai is a tone language in which every syllable carries a lexical tone; stress is not contrastive. Within a polysyllabic morpheme, a compound or a reduplicate, the non-final syllable(s) are stress-reduced (first degree: vowel quality kept, length neutralised, sandhi tone; second/extreme degree: final consonant lost, vowel becomes short /a/, all tonal contrast lost = 'neutral tone'), while the final syllable is fully stressed and carries the canonical tone. Prominence is therefore rightmost/final within the word or close-knit phrase. Diller 1989 (Sathing Phra, Songkhla) independently states that stress 'should be considered secondary or non-contrastive' and that unmarked syllables are 'unstressed variable-pitch' (neutral-tone-like) syllables; Diller 1979a notes that initial syllables of bisyllabic lexemes are 'lightly-accented' and are regularly deleted (apheresis) in rural Southern Thai.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed as such; Court distinguishes only fully stressed vs. two degrees of non-fully stressed syllables.
new_statements.exceptions: Court: a few Malay loanwords with irregular (non-sandhi) tones in penult (p.73). Diller 1989: stress features of deictic Groups II and IV are variable; Group I deictics form the stress peak of the utterance.
new_statements.domain_note: Court describes stress reduction within polysyllabic morphemes (mostly Malay loans), compounds, reduplicates and 'close-knit phrases' — i.e. word/phonological-phrase level, not citation monosyllables; Diller 1989's remarks are about deictic words in connected speech.
new_statements.identity_note: The deciding source (Court 1975) describes Satun Thai, the Southern Thai dialect of Satun province spoken by ethnically Malay speakers on the western coast, which Court calls 'a typical Pak Tai (southern Thai) dialect'; Diller 1989 describes the Sathing Phra (Songkhla) rural dialect; Diller 1979a covers rural vs. urban Southern Thai generally. All fall under sout2746 (no separate glottocode for Satun or Songkhla Thai). Glottolog's Saiegh-Haddad 2011 reference is a misattribution (Arabic).

new_statements.quote: Diller (1985:342) points out that the change in tone AB1 is a gradual north-to-south progression from high falling [52] to higher-mid rising falling [452/453/454] to high rising [45]. Thirty years ago, tone AB1 was pronounced as high falling [52] in the northern area of Southern Thailand, while in the southern area, it was pronounced as high falling [52] for unstressed syllables and as higher-mid rising falling [452/453/454] for stressed syllables. Subsequently, the higher-mid rising falling [452/453/454] tone began to be pronounced as higher-mid rising [45] for stressed syllables by some younger speakers in Songkhla. In this century, most Songkhla speakers pronounce tone AB1 as higher-mid rising [45] for both stressed and unstressed syllables.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog record (Court 1975: tone language in which non-fully-stressed, non-final syllables show reduced/sandhi tones and full tones occur on stressed syllables) and with the Diller 1985 'notes on stress' entry already read: Phonyarit likewise treats tonal realisation as conditioned by stressed vs unstressed syllables. It adds no placement information (silent on position, weight, secondary stress), so it neither refines nor contradicts the fixed: final syllable pattern on record.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The article is a tone-geography survey elicited with 80 monosyllabic words (Gedney checklist) from 998 speakers; it has no section on stress and states no stress-placement rule. Its only stress content is incidental: following Diller (1985:342) it reports that in southern Southern-Thai areas tone AB1 formerly had different realisations in stressed ([452/453/454]) and unstressed ([52]) syllables, and that most present-day Songkhla speakers use [45] in both. It thus presupposes a stressed/unstressed syllable distinction that conditions tonal realisation, but says nothing about where stress falls. Satun localities are assigned to regional tone dialects 7 (Lower Western: West La Ngu, West Tha Phae), 8 (Central: East La Ngu, East Tha Phae, Thung Wa, Ma Nang, Khuan Kalong, Mueang Satun) and 9 (Lower Eastern: Khuan Don) (Table, p.9-10).
new_statements.exceptions: none; the other 'accent' hits (journal p.24, p.29) mean regional accent, not word accent
new_statements.identity_note: The article covers all of Southern Thai (14 provinces, 998 speakers) and classifies it into nine regional tone dialects; Satun province localities fall into dialect 7 Lower Western (West La Ngu, West Tha Phae), dialect 8 Central (East La Ngu, East Tha Phae, Thung Wa, Ma Nang, Khuan Kalong, Mueang Satun) and dialect 9 Lower Eastern (Khuan Don). The stressed/unstressed remark concerns the 'southern area' and Songkhla speakers, not Satun specifically. The catalog record (Court 1975) describes Satun Thai proper.

tone_statements.quote: The theoretical framework of this study was based on Gedney's tone box theory (Gedney, 1972). The phonetic characteristics of the tones are based on auditory judgment and confirmed by an acoustic study. In addition, the Praat program was used to analyze the fundamental frequency and the phonetic characteristics were shown in the semitone scale. The study showed that age influenced the tone variation and the tendency of tone change. [...] Furthermore, the tone system was found to be the same in all locations. The phonetic characteristics of the tones differ when occurring in different areas and it was concluded that the phonetic characteristics of tones vary by region. It was also established that there are 6 sub-dialects spoken in Songkhla.

tone_statements.summary: Lexical tone system of Songkhla Southern Thai (Gedney tone-box splits/mergers uniform across the province); phonetic realisations vary by area and age; inventory size not stated in the abstract (Songkhla is in the 7-tone zone per the known literature).

tone_statements.citation: Egerod, Søren. 1972. The tones of Phuket and Ko Samui: a correction. In Jimmy G. Harris & Richard B. Noss (eds), Tai Phonetics and Phonology, 50-51. Bangkok: Central Institute of English Language, Mahidol University.
tone_statements.quote: In Egerod (1961), I recorded the tones of Phuket as being identical with those of Nakhonsithammarat, and those of Ko Samui as being identical with both of these in categories (tonemes) but not in tonal manifestations. [...] [p.50, after the Phuket chart:] The two main differences from Nakhonsithammarat in development of tonemes (categories, not manifestations) are that MG is not identical with M:G, but that on the other hand M2 and H2 have coalesced. [p.51, after the Ko Samui chart:] Ko Samui is then different from both Phuket and Nakhonsithammarat in combining M2 and LI (like Standard Thai, but without adding H2); but like Nakhonsithammarat, different from Phuket, H2 and M2 are kept apart. In actual manifestation the Ko Samui tone /me/ is higher than mid, but not as high as /he/. I was happy to find that Brown (1965: pp. 122-123) has come to exactly the same conclusion. So there is no longer any discrepancy between Dr. Brown's and my own description of the Southern Thai tones.
tone_statements.summary: Phuket and Ko Samui Southern Thai: six contrastive tones on live syllables (high-falling, mid-rising-falling, low-falling, low-rising, mid-level, low-level), distributed over the Gedney-type box by initial class and tone category; the two dialects differ in the category membership of M2 (Phuket M2=H2 mid-level; Samui M2=L1 low-rising) and of long dead M-syllables.

sources.note: Satun Thai (a 'typical Pak Tai' dialect): tones a-n occur in fully stressed syllables, sandhi tones o-s in non-fully-stressed syllables before a fully stressed one (p.70); section 'Tone sandhi and stress reduction' (p.72): first element of a compound or reduplicate is stress-reduced, two degrees of reduction (2nd degree = vowel to short /a/, all tone lost, 'neutral tone'); non-final syllables of polysyllabic morphemes are subject to stress reduction (p.73). Stress itself is not treated as contrastive.

sources.quote: In Egerod (1961), I recorded the tones of Phuket as being identical with those of Nakhonsithammarat, and those of Ko Samui as being identical with both of these in categories (tonemes) but not in tonal manifestations. [...] [p.50, after the Phuket chart:] The two main differences from Nakhonsithammarat in development of tonemes (categories, not manifestations) are that MG is not identical with M:G, but that on the other hand M2 and H2 have coalesced. [p.51, after the Ko Samui chart:] Ko Samui is then different from both Phuket and Nakhonsithammarat in combining M2 and LI (like Standard Thai, but without adding H2); but like Nakhonsithammarat, different from Phuket, H2 and M2 are kept apart. In actual manifestation the Ko Samui tone /me/ is higher than mid, but not as high as /he/. I was happy to find that Brown (1965: pp. 122-123) has come to exactly the same conclusion. So there is no longer any discrepancy between Dr. Brown's and my own description of the Southern Thai tones.
sources.note: Gives full tone charts (Thai orthographic initial class H/M/L x tone category 0, 1 [mai ek], 2 [mai tho], dead short G, dead long:G, with tone values coded h/m/l + e even / r rising / f falling) for Phuket and for Ko Samui. Phuket live syllables: H0=H1 hf, H2 me, M0=M1 mrf, M2 me, L0 lf, L1 lr, L2 le (six tonemes: hf, mrf, lf, lr, me, le); dead: H he/me, M mr/me, L le/lr. Versus Nakhon Si Thammarat, Phuket keeps MG distinct from M:G but merges M2 with H2. Ko Samui: same as Phuket except M2 = lr (merged with L1, as in Standard Thai but without H2) and M:G = lr; H2 and M2 kept apart as in Nakho…
